queue.title: AI Could Bring Back the Dark Ages
queue.dek: The debate over AI is framed as regulation versus free markets. But the real question is whether elected governments can retain control over technologies that threaten civilization itself, writes Elliot Ackerman.
queue.opening: Over the past several months, as artificial intelligence and its potentially catastrophic effects on society have taken center stage, discussion around the technology has broken down along a familiar framework in American politics, dividing into two camps: pro-regulation versus pro–free market. On the one hand, you have researchers like David Robinson , a senior safety leader at OpenAI, who after resigning from his position two weeks ago wrote that “the future depends on the wisdom that Silicon Valley lacks.” Joining him are tech industry leaders like Bill Gates, who recently warned that “AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths.” This camp argues for greater government oversight over AI, and for AI companies to proceed more cautiously. On the other hand, you have people like President Donald Trump, who has called demands for AI regulation a “hoax.” He has led an equally loud chorus, which includes tech leaders like Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, who argue that concerns about AI are overblown and disingenuous, that AI leaders like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei are eager for regulation so that they can box out competition, and that pumping the brakes on AI amounts to government meddling in the free market. queue.dek: The $25 billion penalty comes after jurors found Meta committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws.
queue.opening: Meta Platforms has been ordered to pay $25 billion after a New Mexico jury found the company misled Facebook users over its handling of personal data and other practices in a case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal. New Mexico Judge Francis Mathew issued the penalty Wednesday after jurors found last month that Meta made dozens of misleading statements to users. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Mathew wrote in his order. The now-defunct Cambridge Analytica, which worked for President Donald Trump's 2016 campaign, obtained information from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app without their consent. META PUTS POPULAR NEW TOOL IN HANDS OF SMALL BUSINESSES New Mexico sued Meta in 2021, accusing the company of misleading users about who could access their personal information and how it handled harmful content on the platform. Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements examined during the trial were misleading and determined that Meta committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws. Mathew said the violations could have resulted in a penalty of more than $219 billion under state law but ultimately reduced the amount to $25 billion. queue.dek: The Department of Energy plans to loan 315,000 barrels from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve as fuel oil prices surge 70% from a year ago.
queue.opening: The Department of Energy (DOE) on Wednesday announced plans to loan up to about one-third of the U.S. emergency heating oil reserve in an effort to ease price pressures facing consumers as global conflicts constrain energy supplies. The announcement indicated that the DOE will loan up to 315,000 barrels of fuel oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate supply disruptions. The reserve holds a supply of one million barrels of ultra-low sulfur distillate, which serves as heating oil, at four locations in the Northeast due to the popularity of heating oil as a significant source of home heating in the region. Under the terms of the DOE's request for proposal, companies that borrow from the reserve in the 2026-27 heating season must return the same volume of oil plus a premium to refill the reserve before the 2027-28 heating season. "The Trump administration is committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs for the American people," said Energy Secretary Chris Wright. "After receiving Senators Collins' and Kings' letter and extensive discussions with Senator Collins, I have directed the Department to exchange barrels from our Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate heightened home heating oil costs during the upcoming winter."
